extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary history and comparative medieval literature
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the qualities and standards by which heroic and medieval literature (poetry, language, and historical transmission) are judged — e.g., subject matter, narrative technique, style, language choice, and preservation. The excerpt is a lecture on the Nibelungenlied and broader principles of literary value in the Middle Ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper subjects of heroic poems
rubrics_metrics.description: “The proper subjects of all heroic poems — the fall of nations, and the contest of heroes,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic poetry should treat grand themes (national catastrophe, heroic combat). The lecture cites the opening stanza of a panegyric to show how such lofty subjects are signalled even when the poem appears to have a different ostensible subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilful unfolding of incidents and dramatic vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: “That skilful unfolding of incidents, and almost dramatic vividness of representation which form the chief characteristic of the Homeric poems,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong heroic/narrative poem should unfold incidents with dramatic momentum and vivid representation. The Homeric model is named as an ideal of incident-unfolding and theatrical vividness; other traditions may imitate this with varying success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plan; sequential pictorial structure
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is peculiarly distinguished by its unity of plan; it is a picture, or rather it is a series of successive pictures, each naturally following the other,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A heroic poem ought to exhibit a coherent unity of design—either as a single picture or as a sequence of interlinked scenes that follow naturally. The Nibelungenlied is praised for this structural unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness and simplicity; avoidance of superfluities
rubrics_metrics.description: “All delineated with great boldness and simplicity, and a total disregard of all superfluities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective heroic poetry favors bold, simple expression and economy — cutting away ornament that does not serve the narrative or emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language vitality: liveliness, strength, flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “The German language appears in this work in a state of perfection ... possessed a flexibility ... along with all its natural liveliness and strength,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style and diction should show linguistic vitality — liveliness, strength, and flexibility — enabling clear, forceful portrayal. The lecture contrasts such living language with later affectation and hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic archetype: youthful hero and tragic destiny
rubrics_metrics.description: “The interest turns on the fate of a youthful hero, who is represented as invested with all the attributes of beauty, magnanimity, and victory — but dearly purchasing all these perishable glories by the certainty of an early and a predicted death.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic narratives often center on an idealized young champion whose virtues and glory are offset by inevitable tragic fate; this contrast is central to emotional and thematic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of death with solemnity, stillness, and tenderness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The death of the German hero ... has in it more solemnity and stillness, and is withal depicted with more exquisite touches of tenderness,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes of death in heroic poetry should convey solemnity and restraint, using delicate touches to evoke pathos rather than sensational violence; comparison to Homer indicates different aesthetic choices for such scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety: full representation of joyful and sorrowful life
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Nibelungen-lied is, moreover, a poem abounding in variety; in it both sides of human life, the joyful as well as the sorrowful, are depicted in all their strength.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great heroic poem balances tonal variety — feasting and love as well as combat and mourning — thereby fulfilling promises made in opening stanzas and giving the work emotional breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfilling the opening stanza’s promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation: “I sing of loves and wassellings ... Of bold men's bloody combatings, and gentle ladies' tears.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poem should deliver on the elements it promises at the outset; an opening that signals both festivity and battle should be matched by content that includes both. This is a standard of narrative honesty and structural expectation-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention precedes refinement; legend before history, poetry before criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every where ... the fulness of invention must precede the refinements of art, — legend must go before history, and poetry before criticism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative work must begin with imaginative, original invention; formal refinement and analytical critique come later. This is a developmental criterion for national literatures and for nurturing original poetic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical antiquity necessary for national character
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the literature of any nation has had no such poetical antiquity before arriving at its period of regular and artificial development, we may be sure that this literature can never attain to a national shape and character,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A living national literature is built on an earlier period of popular/poetical tradition; authors should draw on and cultivate vernacular poetic roots to achieve distinctive national expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as organ of tradition and transmitter of ancient knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Literature ... may also be regarded ... as the great organ of tradition, by means of which the knowledge of the ancient world is transmitted to the modern,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aside from invention, literary production is judged by its capacity to preserve, transmit, and augment inherited knowledge and cultural memory; writers serving this role should balance fidelity to sources with living expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer vernacular for poetic vitality; danger of translating into a dead language
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many poetical monuments ... have perished, in consequence of the pains taken by well-meaning translators ... in rendering every thing into Latin, and clothing what was originally true poetry and heroic legend, in the disguises of dull prose,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating vernacular poetry into a dead or foreign learned tongue can strip it of life; poets and editors should preserve works in living vernaculars to maintain their poetic effect. This is an anti-pattern warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual choice of language: necessity of a common language in early periods
rubrics_metrics.description: “Before the several dialects now in use had acquired some degree of precision and refinement, a common language was absolutely necessary ... for the purposes of religious worship, learning, and education,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language choice is pragmatic: a lingua franca (even a ‘dead’ language) may be necessary for certain institutional functions. Authors must weigh audience, function, and stage of linguistic development when choosing language for composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and transmission as a literary duty
rubrics_metrics.description: “To preserve the writings of the ancient authors was not barely considered as a matter of duty, but formed the most favourite exercise of monastic skill.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copying, collecting, and transmission of texts is a recognized moral and cultural duty; the survival and influence of literature depend on such preservation efforts, so curatorial practices affect literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and perspicuity as key qualities of good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “That the authors of the eleventh century wrote more agreeably and perspicuously in Latin than those of the latest Roman age ... In all those qualities of good writing which are attainable by men composing in a dead language, their superiority is most evident.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreeable, perspicuous expression (clarity, readability) is a central standard for judging prose and learned composition; even when using an archaic or learned language, writers should aim for lucidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of preserving scientific and technical knowledge within literary culture
rubrics_metrics.description: “Next to language and its monuments, nothing else was of so great importance as the preservation of the mathematics, which are the foundation of all knowledge of nature,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A culture’s literary and scholastic output is judged also by its attention to preserving and teaching sciences and technical arts; literary institutions that support mathematical and technical learning are credited with broader civilizational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial conditions suited to historical writing: independence and reflective retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps the very best of all situations for a writer of history is one ... in which he enjoys abundant opportunities of gaining experimental knowledge of men and their affairs, but is at the same time independent of the world and its transactions, and has full liberty to mature in retirement his reflections ... Such was the situation of many of those German historians ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good historical writing benefits from a balance of access to real-world affairs and the independence to reflect; the institutional condition of many monastic historians is offered as a model rather than a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the processes of vernacular formation; practical advice on language cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a thing infinitely more easy to cultivate at the same time two languages radically distinct, than to give a new form to a language which has either been changed by some internal revolution, or mingled ... That must always be a work of great labour and patience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When nurturing a vernacular literary tradition, authors and cultural planners should recognize that forming or reforming a language is slow and laborious; strategies that cultivate multiple languages may be more feasible than radical internal reform.
